subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The Expanding Universe
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Expanding Universe.

hook.text: In 1929, Edwin Hubble discovered that galaxies are flying apart. The farther away, the faster they recede.

buildup.text: He measured redshift—light stretched to longer wavelengths by the expansion of space—in dozens of galaxies.

discovery.text: This meant the universe is expanding. Run the clock backward and everything converges to a single point.

twist.text: Einstein had added a term to keep his equations static. He called it his 'biggest blunder' after Hubble proved him wrong.

climax.text: The Hubble constant measures the expansion rate. Pinning down its exact value remains one of cosmology's biggest debates.

punchline.text: Galaxies racing apart. The universe has been growing since birth.

quiz.question: What did Hubble's observations of galaxy redshifts reveal?
options: The universe is expanding, with galaxies moving apart from each other
Galaxies are rotating around a central point
Light from distant galaxies is being absorbed by dust

details.summary: The universe has been expanding since the Big Bang — galaxies are moving apart as space itself stretches. Edwin Hubble discovered in 1929 that more distant galaxies recede faster, establishing Hubble's Law.
details.whyItMatters: The expanding universe is the central observation of modern cosmology. It implies the universe had a beginning (the Big Bang) and has a future — whether eternal expansion, contraction, or something else entirely.
takeaways: Space itself stretches, carrying galaxies apart over time
Hubble discovered more distant galaxies recede faster
Expansion implies the universe had a finite beginning

faq.question: Does the expansion of the universe affect us locally?
faq.answer: No. Gravity holds together structures like galaxies, solar systems, and atoms. Expansion only dominates on the largest scales, between galaxy clusters. The Milky Way and Andromeda are actually approaching each other due to gravity. Expansion matters only where gravity doesn't bind objects together.

faq.question: What is the expansion rate of the universe?
faq.answer: The Hubble constant is approximately 70 km/s per megaparsec — meaning a galaxy 1 megaparsec (3.26 million light-years) away recedes at 70 km/s. The exact value is debated (the 'Hubble tension'): CMB measurements give about 67, while local measurements give about 73.
